As many of you know, Sanders and a few other democratic representatives are introducing a bill to increase the federal minimum wage to $15 per hour. The timing of this bill is of course meant to help rally his base, but in the interest of critical thought and intellectual honesty, it's important to discuss possible beneficial AND negative consequences of such legislation.

In the past, the minimum wage was meant to provide the means for a minimum standard of living. With how our economy has changed so much, and the meteoric rise of the Mc-job, I think it can be agreed that the minimum wage no longer fills this goal. Should we reconsider the "purpose" of minimum wage in the 21st century or strictly adhere to its original design?
What are you arguments for AND against a minimum wage increase?

Arguments for a higher minimum wage:

  • It will redistribute income from business owners to workers and more income for workers will lead to greater spending in the overall economy

  • It allows business to collude (via the government) to keep wages low, which would be illegal absent the government involvement

  • It will reduce government spending on income assistance

  • It will encourage more people to join the labor force which will provide more workers and grow the economy

Arguments against a higher minimum wage:

  • It will result in job losses for people employed at the minimum wage

  • It will cause businesses to replace minimum wage workers with automated equipment

  • It will cause business to raise prices which will cause inflation

  • It will cause some business to fail which will cause job losses for people employed at minimum wage
Do you really think it'll reduce government spending on income assistance? Right under that it says it will result in job losses, meaning more people on medicaid and other government aid.

Personally, I'm skeptical there will be much short term job loss with a modest increase in minimum wage and I doubt the decrease in government spending on income assistance will be noticeable. Both arguments are being used against or for an increase in minimum wage so I thought I'd pass them along.

In the /v/news thread someone posted a few links to university studies that showed that an increased minimum wage will not have any significant effect on unemployment rates whatsoever. Also there has to be some reason why countries with a high minimum wage have lower poverty and unemployment rates.
I think it'll force inflation of everything, resulting in the new minimum wage being the same value that it is now.

Some of your arguments are directly contradictory. For instance, increasing the minimum wage cannot both provide more workers and result in job losses - that just doesn't make sense. Personally, I think that while raising the minimum wage might encourage more people to prefer minimum wage employment to unemployment, the job opportunities simply will not be available due to widespread layoffs in minimum wage industries. Companies have demonstrated in the past that when the costs of doing business go up, the brunt of the burden falls to the lowest level employees. For example, when the Affordable Care Act went into effect, I was working for Jimmy Johns. As a result of that legislative measure, Jimmy Johns instituted a strict new part-time policy limiting all hourly employees to 25 hours/week in order to avoid offering us insurance.

They are directly contradictory; I was showing both sides of the argument. They can't both be true, but until we raise the minimum wage we won't know which arguments are true and which aren't.

No doubt companies will try to avoid the minimum wage, but they still need to produce products or services if they want to stay in business. Widespread layoffs simply won't happen in the short term. In the medium term, companies will compare the cost of employees with the cost of automation and that's where my concern lies. The cost of capital is close to zero and if employees become more expensive that will lead to automation replacing employees at a faster pace.

Since the costs of automation are basically guaranteed to keep declining as technology improves, isn't this inevitable? I agree completely. What does society look like then? How many wage earners can become advertisers, artists, actors, or musicians? I think they wealthy continue to gain wealth but what happens to the rest of us?

Honestly, I don't see any reason why society couldn't see a total shift within the next 200 years to an entirely service-based economy. I envision a nation in which there are six primary job sectors:

  1. Robot control. These people own the means of production, both of raw materials and consumer goods. They control the machines responsible for doing every type of manual labor imaginable, design and program new machines, and sell robots for professional and personal use.
  2. Personal services. These people do everything that robots and computers cannot do. They are doctors, teachers, lawyers, etc. Additionally, every robot-dominated industry will need service representatives to deal with consumers face to face.
  3. Entertainment and media. These people create their own supply and demand. They provide leisure activities and products, because as the amount of work required of individuals decreases with technological increases, we will all have much more free time.
  4. Advertising. As I mentioned before, advertising will only become more important with time. Alternately, advertisers may become "public relations managers" for companies, not only promoting their products but also working to redeem brand credibility in the wake of major mistakes.
  5. Science. Pushing the boundaries of what we know and what we can do (or what we can program robots to do for us). Primarily they would focus most heavily on space exploration, though a good number would need to be employed by robot companies to continue improving robotic technology, as mentioned above.
  6. Government. It's not going away, but hopefully its focus will change from policing citizens to protecting them (but I digress).

minimum wage is inherently flawed ab initio as follows: when you create a minimum wage, you create built-in costs for production, wholesale and retail distribution. at all levels before the product hits the consumers, the owners will compensate for those built-in costs by passing on the cost to the next level, on an ever-growing basis. so, the manufacturer passes on the cost to the wholesaler. (this doesn't even take into account any third party costs for shipping, packaging, etc. or the parts manufacturers, etc. - but that hidden cost is included.) the wholesaler passes on the additional costs from the manufacturer plus his own additional cost from his own labor, to the retailer. the retailer bundles all of these costs together with his own costs and passes them onto the consumer. the consumer who makes minimum wage complains that he cannot afford these products so the government is forced to raise minimum wage. once that happens, the manufacturer passes on the cost to the wholesaler...

the ideal situation is to not have a minimum wage and let market forces determine the value of work performed, as is done is the other sectors of employment (e.g., non-minimum wage jobs). we would see a ripple effect of prices dropping (making food and other products affordable to the would-be minimum wage workers) not just because the costs of getting the products to consumers drops, but because in order to be able to sell the products to minimum wage workers, retailers would have to price the products accordingly.

of course, none of this is possible in a society that already has a minimum wage in place. the cycle has already begun and we cannot get ourselves out from under it. so, we've no choice but to raise the minimum wage and continue the never-ending dog and cat chase of minimum wage v. cost of living.

FOR:

Plenty of people cannot afford the basic costs of living anymore. As a single father with two children I would not be able to provide for them should I suddenly find myself having to work for minimum wage. Add to that the health and nutrition benefits of an increased wage. Providers are able to afford costlier, healthier alternatives to the cheap-as-can-be processed junk that they are currently left to feed their family.

As an example; I can buy a head of lettuce, some tomatoes, some cucumbers, and some salad dressing for a family of three and it costs me approximately $10. This will provide my children and I a side dish for possibly 2 meals.

I can buy 6 to 10 boxes of macaroni & cheese mix for about the same amount of money. That will provide a side dish for my children and I for an entire week.

On an extremely tight budget it's understandable why a family depending on minimum wage, as it currently stands, would opt for the less expensive (and far less healthy) options.

AGAINST:

When the cost of labor rises for the lowest paid earners in society it has minimal effect on the people marginally above their tier of pay. If I make one dollar an hour more than the lowest paid employee an increase in the minimum wage (of this magnitude) will also increase my pay but not by the same margin. So instead of making, say, 5% above minimum I'm now making 2%. Furthermore, the higher above the minimum base that you are the worse it becomes. At some point your wages will not be increased at all. So increasing the minimum wage devalues the wages of all people above minimum with the highest paid earners suffering the most.

And with an increase in minimum wage those prices for salad, and the price of that mac and cheese, all must go up in order for companies to afford the labor needed to produce those products. So it temporarily increases the income of the lowest paid earners but, eventually, leaves us no better off than we are now. And some of us are worse for the wear. Take the person earning $20 per hour right now. They make a nice amount of money over the current minimum. If the minimum is raised to $15, how much of an increase will that person receive? My guess is that it will not be much, if any at all. The base-line for cost of living has risen. And now you've got a worker who can no longer afford the healthy food options that they were once able to afford. Their standard of living must decrease.

It's good intentioned to increase the income of the poorer among us but in the long term we've only created more poor.

These are the arguments I like:

For - $10/hr - this keeps pace with the min wage back from the 60s and is simply an update to the system.

For - $15/hr - it converts the poorest of our nation from benefit recipients to low middle class consumers which generate further economic growth and allegedly many jobs that pay around 15/hr will increase their wages to compete.

Con - $9/hr - the economy is still recovering and doesn't need any further upsets (I don't really buy into this one myself - I think it's just asshole speak for "I want more money for myself").

Con - $15/hr - Min wage employees now earn as much as some skilled labor. This creates a communist like incentive to work as little as you can into our economy. It also allows min wage employees to directly compete for resources with people who have more professional jobs (housing, clothing, etc - more demand = higher price).

Minimum wages hurt poor people, the very people they're intended to benefit. When the cost to produce a good or service increases, businesses pass along the expense to consumers by raising their prices. The net result of this is higher prices across the board, an increased cost of living proportionate to the minimum wage increase.

They also hurt the employability of unskilled workers. Why would a business pay an unskilled person $15/hr for a job when the same amount of money will afford someone with skills and experience? What if you're that unskilled worker, desperate for a job and willing to work for less if it means you'll get hired? Not an option. Without the ability to work for less, there's no way for you to make yourself more hireable in a competitive job market.

Finally, employment is an agreement between employer and employee. It's a two-party contract, which either party can voluntarily break from if they're unhappy with it. No outside parties have any business interfering with the terms of that contract. If Company X wants to pay its workers nothing it has every right to try that... but I doubt anyone will be interested in the job. The negotiation of wages is a natural market force whereby employers and employees agree on the value of the work being done. If the employee feels underpaid, or the employer is overpaying, either one ought to be able to terminate employment or amend its terms in order to find something that will meet their needs better.

When two parties meet to contract voluntarily and no one else is harmed, it's unethical for a third party to interfere and demand changes to the terms of their agreement. Even if that third party has the best of intentions.

Minimum wage increase pros and cons. Pro: We will no longer be working odd crappy hours for low wages. We can finally be out of the 1970's living minimum wages. More Part time jobs. Con: Possible more mom and pop business closures. Fewer full time jobs.

If you want people to have more money, that's fine. The best way to do it it to reduce taxes for companies that comply and then divert budget from other areas of the government and increase welfare benefits to those that qualify.

It's that simple. Of course, this means that the government is taking the hit instead of the public, so, it's highly unlikely.

But since there is no way to separate those jobs, I guess I'm for it.
